title: Pasta alla Genovese
subtitle: Neapolitan pasta with slow-cooked onion and beef sauce
excerpt: A Neapolitan classic where a large amount of onion is cooked with beef for several hours until both melt into a sweet, thick sauce. The onion is the star, not the meat.
sourceNotes: Pasta alla Genovese is a Neapolitan dish despite its name. The slow-cooked onion and beef ragu is a Naples Sunday tradition.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the sauce for up to 3 months. The beef can be sliced and served separately as a second course.
recipe.batchNotes: The sauce is already a large batch recipe. It keeps in the fridge for 4 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the sauce 1 or 2 days ahead. The flavour deepens considerably overnight.

content.text: Pasta alla Genovese takes patience but not much skill. A very large quantity of onion collapses over 3 hours into a pale, sweet, jammy sauce. Do not try to speed it up. High heat makes the onions bitter.
Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy pot over a medium heat. Add the carrot and celery. Cook for 5 minutes until softened.
Add all the onions and the salt. The pot will be very full. Stir to combine. Cover and cook on a low heat for 30 minutes until the onions wilt and release their liquid.
Remove the lid. Nestle the beef into the onions. Add the white wine and bay leaves. Stir gently.
Cook uncovered on the lowest heat for 2 to 2.5 hours. Stir every 20 minutes. The onions should slowly turn pale golden and jammy. The beef will become very tender.
Lift the beef out. Pull it apart into large shreds with two forks. Return the shreds to the sauce. Remove the bay leaves.
Cook the pasta in well-salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve a mugful of pasta water. Drain and add to the sauce.
Toss everything together over a low heat with a splash of pasta water. Serve in bowls with parmesan and a grind of black pepper.

items.symptom: The onions have browned and turned bitter.
items.cause: The heat was too high during the long cook.
items.fix: Keep the flame at its very lowest. The onions should sweat and collapse, not fry. Add a splash of water and stir if they are catching.

items.symptom: The beef is still tough after 2 hours.
items.cause: The heat was not consistent or the cut was too lean.
items.fix: Continue cooking for another 30 minutes on a very low heat. Chuck needs time for its connective tissue to soften.

items.symptom: The sauce is too liquid at the end.
items.cause: The lid was left on too long, preventing evaporation.
items.fix: Cook uncovered for a final 20 minutes on a medium-low heat until the sauce tightens to a jammy consistency.
